Authors present a semi-supervised learning method for medical image
segmentation. The main novelty is to use SAM to this end. In an
elegant approach, authors first fine-tune two SAM models. The first -
bigger one - is updated with low parameter updates, while the second -
the smaller one - is updated completely. After fine-tuning,
semi-supervised learning happens in a teacher-student setup. However,
in their setup, authors use distillation and freeze the teacher
network - the bigger SAM. Distillation works both on the output but
also on the embedding space.

Experiments with three important benchmark datasets are
presented. Results are quite promising for the proposed
approach. Ablation studies are also conducted. They show the imprtance
of fine-tuning of the student model as well as using two losses during
knowledge distillation. The contribution of the dynamic loss weighting
remains minimal, however, the presence of this experiment is valuable.

The main concerns are related to the level of novelty and the fact
that the student and teacher models are fine-tuned on the same
dataset. However, despite these concerns, three out of four reviewers
praise the contribution and acknowledge that this would lead to
further work and interesting discussions at the conference. One
reviewer remains rather negative about the article, however, I do not
share the concerns of this reviewer about the article.

**Summary**: I find this article to be a solid contribution. While the
  novelty in terms of technical components may not be very high, the
  approach is still novel for semi-supervised learning, as it utilizes
  SAM models. Furthermore, results on three benchmark datasets are
  quite promising. I believe this article will lead to further
  discussions and interesting future work.

author_final_remarks.value:
We sincerely thank all reviewers (R1: Href, R2: tKUd, R3: yrJD, R4: kvmC) for their time, insightful comments, and recognition of our work.

First, we are encouraged that the reviewers think our work has multiple notable strengths: **(1)** Using efficient SAM as the backbone for semi-supervised medical image segmentation and updating default embeddings to reduce inaccurate prompts are seen as novel (R4) and interesting (R2, R4). **(2)** The fully SAM-based semi-supervised framework and learning strategy, combining feature-level and output-level knowledge distillation, is recognized as making a valuable contribution (R1) and engaging (R4). **(3)** Our paper's motivation is clear (R2), writing is easy to read (R1, R2, R3), and experiments cover diverse imaging modalities and anatomical regions with SOTA results (R1, R2). 

Second, we respond to all concerns raised by reviewers during rebuttal and discussion: **(1)** We emphasize that the novelty of this work lies in the proposed simple and effective framework (focused on problem-level innovation, not just technical details) and learning strategy. We validate effectiveness via ablation studies and compare SAM and MedSAM in our method, which is core to our response to R1. **(2)** For R2's questions on dataset processing, model outputs, prompt encoder, and computational complexity, we provide additional explanations and comparisons, recognized by R2. **(3)** We discuss with R3 the meaning of "semi-supervised" in our method. We carefully explain that our method is a form of semi-supervised segmentation, where labeled data fine-tune the teacher model, and the fine-tuned teacher generates pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, which together with labeled data, train the student model. Moreover, we add new experiments showing unlabeled data's vital role and explain why the student can outperform the teacher. We appreciate R3's insightful questions, which offer valuable inspiration for our research. **(4)** For R4's request for finer dataset details, we provide detailed information on imaging modalities, anatomical regions, pathological diversity, and validate generalizability on a new chest X-ray dataset.

In summary, our research focuses on model distillation under incomplete information, which in a sense is a new task. Based on this work, a series of new works can be derived. We thank the reviewers again for their constructive questions and suggestions, which improve this paper and guide our future research.

Thanks for your patient response again. 

**(1)** In our experiments, the teacher model and the student model indeed use exactly the same labeled data. Please allow us to provide further explanation:

After fine-tuning, the teacher model is frozen and no longer updated. Its role is to extract high-quality "implicit pseudo-labels (excluding the argmax step for generating labels)" from unlabeled data, which is far more than the labeled data. This means the process not only distills existing knowledge from the teacher model to the student model, but also uses these "implicit signals" to supervise the student with much more unlabeled data. Therefore, the amount of data involved in training the student model far exceeds the labeled data alone.

To validate our view, we add the following experiments (see Table 1). Here, **Only Labeled** means the student model is fine-tuned using only labeled data, without any unlabeled data. **Only Unlabeled** means the student model is trained exclusively with "implicit pseudo-labels" extracted from unlabeled data by the fine-tuned teacher model, without any access to labeled data. **Ours** means the final performance of the student model trained using both labeled data and unlabeled data. 

### Table 1: Comparison of student model performance on different training sets using DSC as the evaluation metric.

|Dataset|Labeled Ratio|Only Labeled|Only Unlabeled|Ours|
|-|-|-|-|-|
|LA|5%|79.09|79.08|88.42|
||10%|82.09|83.79|90.47|
|BraTS2019|10%|79.79|78.02|85.14|
||20%|80.60|80.83|86.46|
|PROMISE12|10%|78.17|78.03|83.41|
||20%|80.28|78.15|86.44|

The result shows that these "implicit pseudo-labels" from the teacher model play a non-negligible role in the student model's supervised training on the large amount of unlabeled data. The student model is not merely imitating the teacher's behavior but, guided by these "implicit pseudo-labels", "learns" a better data distribution from more unlabeled data, achieving stronger generalization.

**(2)** Regarding the question "**why the student can outperform the teacher in our method**", we offer the following explanation:

Suppose there are two deep neural network (DNN) models. Model $f_t$ builds an empirical distribution $p_t$ based on only 5% of the training samples to approximate the true distribution $\mathcal{P}_t$. Model $f_s$ builds an empirical distribution $p_s$ using 5% clean samples combined with 95% samples containing bounded noise to approximate $\mathcal{P}_s$. Although the training data of $f_s$ includes a higher proportion of noise, under bounded noise conditions, $p_s$ may approximate the optimal distribution $\mathcal{P}^\star$ better than $p_t$. This phenomenon is not impossible within the framework of statistical learning theory. For example, when the noise level is below a certain threshold, increasing sample diversity can lead to hypotheses obtained by empirical risk minimization (ERM) or regularized ERM (RERM) with lower generalization error bounds. In over-parameterized models, additional samples (even with bounded noise) may improve representation learning and thus enhance generalization performance.

In general, as highly complex machine learning models, DNNs exhibit overfitting tendencies that make the scale of training data a significant factor affecting their performance. In our work, although the teacher model is trained on labeled data and has a larger number of parameters, it only involves a small ratio of the data in the semi-supervised segmentation task. In contrast, the student model involves a significantly larger volume of data than the teacher. Therefore, combined with the previous analysis, it is not unreasonable that the student model outperforms the teacher. 

Moreover, in practical DNN training, model performance is influenced not only by data distribution but also by various other factors. For instance, in our work, key factors include the pretraining strategy of the visual foundation model, such as SAM, fine-tuning methods, such as LoRA, network architectures, such as base vs. tiny, the scale of training samples, and the quality of supervision signals. Due to limited time, we are sorry that we cannot currently provide a fully rigorous theoretical explanation within the scope of our experiments.

**(3)** Thanks again for your insightful comments. 

Your questions have provided important inspiration for our further theoretical exploration. This not only deepens our understanding of the current work but also has the potential to advance related research, particularly model distillation under incomplete information, from a application-driven approach toward a combination of application and theory. Initially, our goal was to achieve an interesting and practical application of visual foundation models in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. However, inspired by your comments, we plan to introduce more systematic theoretical analysis to build a stronger basis for this problem.

Thank you for your patient reply. However, your explanation has not addressed the questions I raised.

First, I would like to confirm a basic issue again: in this paper, do the teacher model and the student model use exactly the same labeled data? If so, the point you mentioned in your response—that "the improvement in the student model's performance stems from effectively leveraging the teacher model's guidance on unlabeled data, which the teacher model itself does not access during its fine-tuning"—in my view, does not constitute a fundamental reason for the student to outperform the teacher. The teacher model itself has strong generalization ability and can directly perform segmentation predictions on unlabeled data, which is precisely what the student model learns during the distillation process. In other words, the knowledge acquired by the student model is essentially just an "imitation of behavior" of the teacher model on unlabeled data, and these behaviors stem from the teacher model's own ability, rather than new capabilities that the student independently learns from unlabeled data.

Therefore, without an increase in supervisory signals (i.e., the labeled data is exactly the same, and what the student learns from the teacher is only what the teacher "already knows"), the student model cannot possibly learn knowledge that "the teacher itself has not yet mastered" from the teacher. Moreover, the student model has a more lightweight architecture and fewer parameters, so in theory, it is even harder for it to exhibit capabilities equivalent to or stronger than those of the teacher.

I am more inclined to believe that the advantage of the student model should lie in the improved efficiency after model compression, rather than in the result of outperforming the teacher in terms of performance.

comment.value:
Thank you for your insightful question. We fully agree with your point that, from a technical perspective, a student model with fewer parameters, trained on the same annotated data as the teacher model, is generally unlikely to outperform the teacher.

As shown in Table 1, when both the teacher and student models are fine-tuned using only the same annotated data, the student model consistently underperforms the teacher across all datasets. This result validates your concern.

### Table 1: Comparison of the fine-tuned performance between teacher and student using DSC as the evaluation metric on the same annotated data.

| Dataset       | Label Ratio | Teacher | Student |
|---------------|-------------|---------|---------|
| LA            | 5%          | 86.22   | 79.09   |
|               | 10%         | 88.54   | 82.09   |
| Brats2019     | 10%         | 84.04   | 79.79   |
|               | 20%         | 85.73   | 80.60   |
| PROMISE12     | 10%         | 85.39   | 78.17   |
|               | 20%         | 86.00   | 80.28   |
| Synapse       | 10%         | 75.99   | 71.84   |

However, in our complete training pipeline, the student model does not rely only on limited annotated data. From a supervision perspective, the teacher model is fine-tuned solely on labeled data, whereas the student model receives supervision from two sources: one is direct supervision from the same labeled data as the teacher, and the other is distillation supervision derived from the teacher model's inference on a large amount of unlabeled data, which produces soft labels and intermediate features used to guide the student at both the output and feature levels. As a result, although the student model has a smaller architecture and fewer parameters, it obtains significantly more supervisory signals than the teacher model that is fine-tuned only on labeled data. This is the key reason why the student model ultimately outperforms the teacher. The improvement in student model's performance is not due to better learning under the same supervision, but rather due to effectively leveraging the teacher's guidance on unlabeled data, which the teacher model itself does not access during its own fine-tuning.

We sincerely hope that our responses have addressed your concerns. Should you have any further questions, we would be more than happy to provide additional clarifications.

title.value: Investigation of MedSAM in our method

comment.value:
Thanks for your recognition and valuable suggestions on our work. 

We carefully investigate the use of MedSAM, a foundation model designed for medical image segmentation, as the starting point of our method, and provide the following additional experiments.

Due to time constraints, we conduct the experiments on the PROMISE12 dataset, as it contains a relatively small amount of data. First, we compare the zero-shot performance of the original SAM used in our method with MedSAM on this dataset (see Table 1), where MedSAM is provided with bounding boxes derived from ground truth as prompts. The results demonstrate the strong generalization capability of MedSAM in medical image segmentation.

### Table 1: Comparison of the zero-shot performance between SAM and MedSAM on the PROMISE12 dataset.

| Method     | DSC ↑  | ASD ↓  |
|------------|--------|--------|
| SAM (Ours) | 2.53   | 94.65  |
| MedSAM     | 66.56  | 10.04  |

Then, we attempt to fine-tune MedSAM on this dataset using the same LoRA-based strategy applied to the original SAM in our method. To ensure a fair comparison, we follow the approach in [1] by not providing any prompts to MedSAM during fine-tuning, since accurate and reliable prompts require specialized medical knowledge. Table 2 presents the comparison results after fine-tuning, where the performance of SAM even surpasses that of MedSAM. 

[1] Li K, Rajpurkar P. Adapting segment anything models to medical imaging via fine-tuning without domain pretraining[C]//AAAI 2024 Spring Symposium on Clinical Foundation Models. 2024.

### Table 2: Comparison of the fine-tuned performance between SAM and MedSAM on the PROMISE12 dataset with 20% labeled data.

| Method     | DSC ↑  | ASD ↓  |
|------------|--------|--------|
| SAM (Ours) | 86.00  | 1.44   |
| MedSAM     | 81.26  | 3.79   |

We attribute this phenomenon to the following reasons: although MedSAM undergoes domain-specific pre-training on medical images, its pre-training dataset size (approximately 1 million images) is considerably smaller than that of SAM, which is pre-trained on a large-scale natural image dataset (approximately 11 million images and 1 billion masks). During the subsequent task-specific fine-tuning stage with limited annotated data, the prior benefits brought by this "small-scale domain pre-training" are likely to be quickly offset by task-driven adaptation, and may even weaken the model's inherent general representation capability. As a result, MedSAM underperforms compared to SAM fine-tuned from scratch. It is possible that fine-tuning MedSAM requires more refined design and optimization strategies. However, due to time constraints, we do not further explore this direction.

Finally, we freeze the fine-tuned MedSAM as the teacher model to further train our efficient student SAM backbone using both labeled and unlabeled data. Table 3 presents the comparison results, showing that using the fine-tuned SAM as the teacher model achieves better performance.

### Table 3: Comparison of the performance between fine-tuned SAM and fine-tuned MedSAM as the teacher model on the PROMISE12 dataset.

| Method     | DSC ↑  | ASD ↓  |
|------------|--------|--------|
| SAM (Ours) | 86.44  | 0.90   |
| MedSAM     | 85.13  | 1.56   |

We sincerely hope that our responses have addressed your concerns. Should you have any further questions, we would be more than happy to provide additional clarifications.

Thank you for your detailed response.

I still have a key question and hope to seek further clarification: In your method, the teacher model is obtained by fine-tuning the original SAM using labeled data; during training, the student model, on the one hand, learns the features and predictions of the teacher model through distillation, and on the other hand, also uses labeled data for direct supervised learning. My question is: **Do the teacher model and the student model use the same annotated data? If they do, why does the student model eventually outperform the teacher model in performance?**

According to my understanding, the learning approaches of the student model in this paper include:
1.Learning from the teacher model;
2.Training using the same annotated data as the teacher model.
Then, without more additional supervisory signals, what the student model learns from the teacher should, in theory, only be what the teacher "has already learned". Furthermore, the teacher model adopts a larger ViT-B architecture, while the student model is a TinyViT with fewer parameters. In terms of the model's expressive capacity, it stands to reason that the student model would find it more difficult to surpass the performance of the teacher model. Therefore, I do not quite understand why the student model would outperform the teacher model on multiple datasets. I hope you can further explain the rationality of this phenomenon.

Thank you again for your patient explanations.

# To Reviewer kvmC

Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comment on our paper.

## Weakness1, Limitation1 and Limitation2: Teacher-student model dependency and SAM's limitations in complex medical scenarios.

Answer: We agree that the performance of the student model can be influenced by the effectiveness of the teacher model. In particular, when dealing with rare pathologies or complex anatomical structures in medical images, the teacher SAM may still face challenges, even after fine-tuning. We have stated these limitations in the Supplementary Material (Section 4) in accordance with the checklist requirements. 
It is important to emphasize that the primary focus of this work is not to enhance SAM's performance in complex medical scenarios, but rather to build an effective and efficient semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework based on it. Perhaps SAM has limitations in extreme cases, but replacing it with a stronger medical-specific model may further improve the performance of our proposed framework.
Moreover, our proposed knowledge distillation strategy helps mitigate the negative impact of imperfect teacher predictions (see Table 1). Specifically, the proposed hierarchical distillation pipeline enables the student model to benefit from multi-level feature transfer, promoting more robust feature representations. In addition, the dynamic loss weighting mechanism gradually reduces the distillation intensity during training, thereby alleviating over-reliance on the teacher and enhancing the student's robustness when encountering challenging or rare cases.
Therefore, although the SAM teacher may introduce some risk of error propagation in extreme scenarios, our method focuses on how to make effective use of powerful foundational models like SAM under practical constraints. We believe this direction is of significant value for advancing semi-supervised medical image segmentation paradigms. In future work, we plan to further explore strategies to reduce the impact of teacher errors on student model optimization.

### Table 1: Comparison between the fine-tuned teacher and the trained student using DSC as the evaluation metric.

| Dataset       | Label Ratio | Teacher | Student |
|---------------|-------------|---------|---------|
| LA            | 5%          | 86.22   | 88.42   |
|               | 10%         | 88.54   | 90.47   |
| Brats2019     | 10%         | 84.04   | 85.14   |
|               | 20%         | 85.73   | 86.46   |
| PROMISE12     | 10%         | 85.39   | 83.41   |
|               | 20%         | 86.00   | 86.44   |
| Synapse       | 10%         | 75.99   | 78.42   |


## Weakness2 and Question1: Description of various medical datasets and detailed fine-grained segmentation results.

Answer: Admittedly, we did not elaborate on the "various medical datasets" used in the abstract. However, the datasets are clearly listed in the Experiments section and further detailed in the Supplementary Material (Section 1). These datasets cover a wide range of imaging modalities, anatomical regions, and pathological conditions, including: contrast-enhanced MRI for left atrial segmentation (LA dataset), multi-modal MRI for brain glioma segmentation (BraTS-2019, using only T2-FLAIR), MRI for prostate segmentation (PROMISE12), and CT for multi-organ abdominal segmentation (Synapse). The Synapse dataset involves eight abdominal organs: aorta, gallbladder, spleen, left kidney, right kidney, liver, pancreas, and stomach. 
The first three datasets focus on single organs such as the left atrium, brain glioma, and prostate, demonstrating our method's effectiveness on these tasks. The fourth dataset is a multi-organ abdominal segmentation dataset, so we provide detailed fine-grained segmentation results for each organ in Table 8 of the paper.
In addition, to verify the generalizability of our method, we introduced a new chest X-ray dataset called CXRS. This dataset contains 1,254 high-resolution chest X-ray images, each annotated at the pixel level with 31 anatomical structures, including 24 ribs, 2 clavicles, 2 scapulae, 2 lungs, and 1 mediastinum. The dataset is split into training, validation, and test sets in a 7:1:2 ratio, comprising 879, 125, and 250 images respectively. Experimental results are shown in Table 2, demonstrating that our method also achieves promising performance on this dataset.

### Table 2: Comparisons with some semi-supervised segmentation methods on the CXRS dataset with 10% labeled data.

| Method   | DSC ↑  | 95HD ↓ |
|----------|--------|--------|
| UA-MT    | 72.14  | 23.69  |
| DTC      | 75.31  | 17.10  |
| BCP      | 78.79  | 10.61  |
| Ours     | 79.45  | 10.32  |

Based on the above studies, our datasets cover three different imaging modalities: MRI, CT, and X-ray. They include a variety of diseases and involve anatomical regions such as the heart, brain, prostate, abdomen, and chest, as well as various detailed subregions. This diversity and representativeness fully support a comprehensive evaluation of the generalizability of our method.


## Question2: Distillation strategy parameters and the dynamic loss weighting schedule.

Answer: Thanks for your reminder and suggestion. We also attach great importance to the configuration setting of the distillation pipeline and the dynamic loss weighting strategy. As shown in Table 4 of the paper and Section 3 of the supplementary material, we conduct an ablation study on the key parameters of the distillation strategy by exploring the loss weight ratio between embedding distillation and output distillation on the LA and PROMISE12 datasets. Based on the results, we adopt the configuration of $\lambda_{emb}$ : $\lambda_{out}$ = 1/3 : 2/3, which also demonstrates stable performance across other datasets. For the dynamic loss weighting strategy, we compare the losses of the teacher and student models and attenuate the distillation intensity only when certain conditions are met [1]. The scaling factor $\alpha$= 0.95 is empirically set and validated through extensive experiments, consistently yielding robust results across different datasets. Therefore, we do not introduce additional automatic tuning mechanisms in this work, nor do we require extensive manual tuning to achieve strong performance, highlighting the generalizability and stability of our method.


## Limitation3: Complexity of hierarchical knowledge transfer and dynamic weighting.

Answer: We acknowledge that introducing hierarchical knowledge distillation and dynamic loss weighting mechanisms increases the model complexity to some extent. However, our method essentially consists of a teacher-student framework, two simple distillation branches, and a dynamic loss weighting mechanism. It involves only a small number of hyperparameters and does not require expert-level tuning. Ablation studies of the paper further demonstrate that these hyperparameters are controllable and easy to adjust. Moreover, our model development was primarily conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU (using two RTX 3090 GPUs for the Synapse dataset), indicating low computational resource requirements. 
Overall, our method is easy to use and easy to generalize, which facilitates its adoption in clinical research and practice.


[1] Huang Y, Wang Y, Tai Y, et al. Curricularface: adaptive curriculum learning loss for deep face recognition[C]//proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2020: 5901-5910.

# To Reviewer yrJD

Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comment on our paper.

## Weakness1: Core Contributions and Innovations.

Answer: The core contribution of the paper lies in exploring how to more effectively apply SAM to semi-supervised medical image segmentation tasks. To this end, we propose a novel fully SAM-based semi-supervised segmentation framework along with a tailored learning strategy. Utilizing unlabeled data for semi-supervised learning is a key component of the proposed strategy. 
Semi-supervised medical image segmentation aims to leverage a small amount of labeled data together with a large amount of unlabeled data for joint training, thereby fully mining the potential information in the unlabeled data. This approach significantly reduces dependence on expert annotations and improves the model's segmentation accuracy and generalization ability. Traditional semi-supervised methods usually rely on consistency regularization or pseudo-labeling mechanisms applied to the unlabeled data, whereas our method adopts a knowledge distillation strategy that enables the student model to effectively benefit from the unlabeled data. Therefore, essentially, our approach is semi-supervised learning.
Specifically:

***(1)*** Our method combines two distillation strategies to supervise labeled data while controlling unlabeled data. This effectively transfers the teacher model's strong segmentation ability to the student model, significantly improving its adaptability to the target domain. And it is a common and effective strategy in semi-supervised medical image segmentation.

***(2)*** In fact, without employing this strategy, effectively leveraging large amount of unlabeled data in the specialized task of semi-supervised medical image segmentation presents considerable challenges, and pseudo-labeling may be the only viable alternative. Notably, in our approach, after the teacher model is fine-tuned and fixed on labeled data, learning from unlabeled data essentially corresponds to a pseudo-label extraction process, although we employ an implicit encoder-decoder form. From this perspective, calculating consistency between the intermediate and output layers of the teacher and student models constitutes a supervised learning process, which constrains the student model's outputs using pseudo-labels (i.e., decoded features) generated by the fixed, powerful pre-trained teacher model.

***(3)*** We input both unlabeled and labeled data into the model simultaneously to jointly train the student encoder-decoder. Since the quantity of unlabeled data far exceeds that of labeled data, its influence on the student model is non-negligible. Experimental results in the paper demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework for utilizing unlabeled data. For example, as shown in Figure 1 of the paper, taking the LA dataset as an instance, we validate the effectiveness of our method. The results indicate that when training the student SAM with only 5% labeled data, the average DSC reaches 79.09%. In contrast, by employing our method with 5% labeled data and 95% unlabeled data, the DSC significantly improves to 88.42%, achieving a gain of 9.33%. This clearly demonstrates that our method's utilization of unlabeled data substantially enhances the performance and generalization ability of the student model.

***(4)*** In our method, supervision of unlabeled data mainly comes from the teacher model. Thus, we provide additional experiments to validate the teacher model's effectiveness (see Table 1).

### Table 1: Comparison between original SAM and fine-tuned SAM using DSC as the evaluation metric. The latter was fine-tuned with 10% labeled data.

| Dataset     | Original SAM | Fine-tuned SAM |
|-------------|---------------|----------------|
| LA          | 17.59         | 88.54          |
| Brats2019   | 6.47          | 84.04          |
| PROMISE12   | 2.53          | 85.39          |
| Synapse     | 3.48          | 75.99          |

Therefore, overall, our method is a semi-supervised medical segmentation approach. In our method, unlabeled data is not merely a medium for distillation but is deeply involved in training the student model, and effectively enhancing the student SAM's adaptation to the target domain.


## Weakness2, Question1 and Question2: Effectiveness of the teacher SAM and comparison between teacher and student.

Answer: We acknowledge that the performance of the teacher model has a significant impact on the effectiveness of distillation, and we recognize the lack of quantitative analysis in the paper regarding the performance difference between the original SAM and the fine-tuned SAM. Although we mentioned in the paper that fine-tuning SAM can improve its performance on medical image segmentation tasks, specific experimental data were not provided. To further validate the effectiveness of the teacher model, we conducted comparative experiments on multiple datasets between the original SAM and the fine-tuned teacher SAM (see Table 1). The results demonstrate that the fine-tuned SAM significantly outperforms the original version across all datasets, confirming its effectiveness as the teacher model. Furthermore, we report the performance gap between the teacher and student models (see Table 2). Experimental results show that, benefiting from abundant unlabeled data and the proposed knowledge distillation-based learning strategy, the student model outperforms the teacher model on most datasets. Notably, our proposed hierarchical distillation pipeline extracts multi-level information to enhance the feature representation capability of the student model. Meanwhile, the dynamic loss weighting strategy gradually reduces the distillation intensity, decreasing the student's reliance on the teacher and partially mitigating the negative impact caused by insufficient teacher performance.

### Table 2: Comparison between the fine-tuned teacher and the trained student using DSC as the evaluation metric.

| Dataset       | Label Ratio | Teacher | Student |
|---------------|-------------|---------|---------|
| LA            | 5%          | 86.22   | 88.42   |
|               | 10%         | 88.54   | 90.47   |
| Brats2019     | 10%         | 84.04   | 85.14   |
|               | 20%         | 85.73   | 86.46   |
| PROMISE12     | 10%         | 85.39   | 83.41   |
|               | 20%         | 86.00   | 86.44   |
| Synapse       | 10%         | 75.99   | 78.42   |


## Question3: Clarification on the role of unlabeled data.

Answer: The term "further optimization" in the paper refers to, based on the fine-tuned teacher model, utilizing unlabeled data together with labeled data to further improve the performance of the student model through semi-supervised learning. In this process, unlabeled data contains a wealth of valuable information that plays a crucial role in improving the overall performance of the student model. Specifically, we transfer the image embeddings and prediction outputs of the unlabeled data from the teacher model to the student model via knowledge distillation, enabling the student to learn richer representations during training. The role of unlabeled data can be further referenced in our response to Weakness1 above.


## Question4: Evaluation of model deployment and storage optimization.

Answer: We place great emphasis on the feasibility of model deployment in practical scenarios. Therefore, in Table 3 of the supplementary material, we present the results of the model complexity comparison experiments. In Table 3, we compare the parameter size (Params) and computational complexity (MACs) between the teacher model based on the original SAM and the efficient student SAM used for inference. The results show that the student model significantly reduces model size and computational cost, with parameters decreasing from 105.05M to 9.51M and MACs from 103.40G to 10.33G, greatly improving inference efficiency. Additionally, Table 8 in the paper also presents a comparison of parameter size between our model and other medical SAM variants based on the original SAM design.


## Question5: Offline distillation's limitation.

Answer: We indeed adopt an offline distillation strategy, wherein the original SAM (ViT-B) is first fine-tuned, then frozen and used as the teacher model to guide the student SAM (TinyViT) during training. Due to the significant architectural differences between the two networks, directly applying soft update strategies such as EMA (Exponential Moving Average) at the parameter level is infeasible, as the parameter dimensions and structures are incompatible and cannot be effectively aligned for updates.
We choose this offline distillation approach because the fine-tuned teacher already possesses strong feature representation capabilities. Meanwhile, we propose a dynamic loss weighting strategy to further mitigate potential mismatches between the fixed teacher and the continuously evolving student. This strategy automatically adjusts the weight of the distillation loss based on the student's learning status, enabling the student to rely more on the teacher's guidance in the early training stage and gradually transition to self-learning in later stages, thereby enhancing the overall effectiveness of the distillation process. In future work, we are also interested in exploring improved learning strategies to further enhance the flexibility of knowledge distillation and the adaptability of the model.

Therefore, comparison with these methods also demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed approach. We will further include the methods listed in Table 1 in the future version of our paper.


## Weakness2: Lack of comparison with medical SAM variants.

Answer: In Table 8 of our paper, we compare our method with several state-of-art medical SAM variants, such as SAMed and H-SAM. We highly acknowledge the contributions of other medical SAM variants like MedSAM and SAM-Med2D to medical image segmentation. These methods significantly enhance the adaptability of SAM to medical tasks through extensive annotated data. However, it is worth noting that the focus of this work lies in exploring the more effective application of SAM in semi-supervised medical image segmentation, rather than merely improving its performance on medical tasks. Therefore, we adopt the original SAM model without complex medical-specific tuning as the initial teacher model, emphasizing innovation at the framework level.
Here, we also provide a comparison with MedSAM (see Table 2), where MedSAM uses ground-truth-derived bounding boxes as prompts.

### Table 2: Comparisons with MedSAM on the Synapse dataset.

| Method   | Aorta | Gallbladder | Kidney(L) | Kidney(R) | Liver | Pancreas | Spleen | Stomach | DSC↑  | 95HD↓  |
|----------|-------|-------------|-----------|-----------|-------|----------|--------|---------|-------|--------|
| MedSAM   | 70.16 | 22.44       | 79.08     | 64.63     | 76.38 | 52.31    | 73.07  | 79.10   | 64.65 | -      |
| Ours     | 86.58 | 67.22       | 83.23     | 79.04     | 93.00 | 57.08    | 86.18  | 75.05   | 78.42 | 17.87  |


## Weakness3: Complexity analysis between SSMIS baselines and Our method.  

Answer: We acknowledge that the paper does not explicitly provide a comparison of model complexity between our proposed method and the SSMIS baselines. It is important to note that SSMIS predominantly employs CNN-based backbone networks, whereas our study is the first to incorporate an efficient SAM as the backbone within the SSMIS framework. Consequently, there exist inherent architectural differences between our approach and the SSMIS baselines. To ensure a fair comparison, we selected representative and high-performing SSL baselines from the current literature for experimental evaluation. Furthermore, to further validate the effectiveness of our method, we supplemented the paper with comparative experiments against several medical SAM variants in Table 8. 
Here, we compare the efficient SAM backbone used in our method with the V-Net backbone commonly adopted in SSMIS baselines. V-Net relies on a 3D convolutional architecture, whose computational complexity can be expressed as:
$$
\mathcal{O}(C^2 \cdot K^3 \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W)
$$
where $C$ denotes the number of channels, $K$ is the kernel size, and $D$, $H$, and $W$ refer to the depth, height, and width of the input volume, respectively. In contrast, our efficient SAM backbone is based on 2D image input and leverages a self-attention mechanism. Its computational complexity is given by:
$$
\mathcal{O}(L \cdot N^2 \cdot d)
$$
where $L$ is the number of transformer layers, $N$ is the number of image patches, and $d$ is the dimension of each token. Moreover, our efficient SAM backbone contains 9.51M parameters, while V-Net has 9.44M parameters.


## Weakness4: Reproducibility details and code.

Answer: In the checklist, we marked "Yes" only for "Experimental result reproducibility," as we have provided extensive implementation details in both the paper and the supplementary material. These include dataset sources, preprocessing procedures, model architecture, training strategies, hyperparameter settings, and evaluation metrics. We are confident that other researchers can reproduce our results based on these settings. Moreover, our method is a simple yet effective framework rather than a complex combination of modules, so it does not require excessive hyperparameter tuning and is easy to implement.
As for the code repository, we marked it as "No" because the code was not fully organized at the time of submission. We have now completed most of the code organization and plan to release it publicly upon paper acceptance. The code repository link will also be included in the final version to further enhance the reproducibility of our method.


## Question1: Processing of the BraTS dataset.

Answer: Our experimental setup on the BraTS 2019 dataset follows the existing semi-supervised medical image segmentation work [1]. We use only the FLAIR modality and merge the edema, NET, and ET regions into a single foreground class to perform a binary segmentation task of the whole tumor. This setup is widely recognized and adopted in semi-supervised segmentation tasks and helps standardize comparison across different studies.


## Question2: Output of mask decoder.

Answer: The mask decoder does not generate multiple masks simultaneously. While the default SAM mask decoder uses multiple mask tokens to predict multiple candidate segmentation results concurrently, in medical scenarios, we follow the modification of the SAM segmentation head proposed in SAMed [2]. Specifically, the mask decoder output is adjusted to produce segmentation maps for k semantic classes (including background), and the final semantic label map is obtained via softmax followed by argmax. Therefore, unlike the VFM setting where the model is trained with one class at a time using binary masks, our model performs multi-class segmentation in a single forward pass.


## Question3: Processing of prompt encoder.

Answer: We use the prompt encoder during mask generation and certainly do not remove it. Specifically, to mitigate the negative effects of inaccurate prompts on SAM's performance, we choose not to provide any prompts, allowing the prompt encoder to generate a default embedding, which is then fed into the mask decoder together with image embedding. During training, we further update this default embedding so that it gradually adapts to the feature distribution of medical images, thereby improving segmentation performance. It is worth noting that the prompt encoder is the key components of SAM, and completely removing it would break the original model architecture and severely degrade overall performance. In contrast, our approach preserves the full structure of SAM while effectively avoiding the negative impact caused by inaccurate prompts.


[1] Luo X, Wang G, Liao W, et al. Semi-supervised medical image segmentation via uncertainty rectified pyramid consistency[J]. Medical Image Analysis, 2022, 80: 102517.

[2] Zhang K, Liu D. Customized segment anything model for medical image segmentation[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2304.13785, 2023.

rebuttal.value:
# To Reviewer Href

Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comment on our paper.

## Weakness1: Limited novelty of combining two well-known distillation strategies.

Answer: Our main contribution lies in the innovation of a semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework, which is designed to be simple and effective. Although our approach indeed combines two existing distillation strategies, feature-level and output-level distillation, we believe that this multi-level distillation strategy offers clear benefits for optimizing the student model. Specifically, output-level distillation offers consistent supervision for the final predictions, while feature-level distillation complements it by aligning intermediate features, facilitating more detailed and stable knowledge transfer. Experimental results across multiple medical datasets validate that this simple design is highly effective in improving model performance. 


## Weakness2: Challenges of comparison with CNN-based SSL baselines.

Answer: Currently, most baseline methods for semi-supervised medical image segmentation are based on CNN backbones. These methods typically achieve high performance and are widely recognized in this field. According to our investigation, although some studies attempt to apply ViT to semi-supervised medical image segmentation (e.g., 3D-ViT), more attention in this area has been given to strategies that combine CNN and ViT, such as SemiCTrans and SemiTC. Considering time constraints and aiming to clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we choose to compare it with the aforementioned approaches. In addition, we extend a representative ViT-based semi-supervised learning method (Semi-ViT) to the medical image segmentation task and compare it with our method under a unified experimental setting (see Table 1).

### Table 1: Comparison with ViT-based methods on the BraTS2019 dataset with 10% labeled data.

| Method       | DSC ↑   | Jaccard ↑ | 95HD ↓ | ASD ↓ |
|--------------|---------|-----------|--------|--------|
| 3D-ViT       | 82.56   | 72.62     | 13.22  | 2.33   |
| SemiTC       | 81.60   | -         | 13.35  | 3.04   |
| SemiCTrans   | 83.62   | 73.06     | 9.42   | 2.63   |
| Semi-ViT     | 81.03   | 70.51     | 15.25  | 4.20   |
| Ours         | 85.14   | 75.56     | 8.58   | 2.57   |

Furthermore, to our knowledge, we are the first to adopt an efficient SAM based on TinyViT as the backbone for a semi-supervised framework. Therefore, we additionally provide comparison experiments between our method and several medical SAM variants in Table 8 of our paper, which indirectly validates the performance advantage of our model over other ViT-based architectures.


## Weakness3: Lack of comparison with recently published papers.

Answer: Thanks for your reminder and suggestion. We will carefully follow recently published papers such as DyCON in our future work.


## Weakness4: Hyperparameter selection process for $\lambda_{out}$ and $\lambda_{emb}$.

Answer: We did perform hyperparameter tuning for $\lambda_{out}$ and $\lambda_{emb}$ using validation sets. Ablation study results on the LA dataset and the PROMISE12 dataset (Section 3 of the supplementary material) indicate that the model achieves optimal performance when $\lambda_{emb}$ : $\lambda_{out}$ is set to 1/3 : 2/3. We did not deliberately tune these hyperparameters for each individual dataset. Instead, we employed a unified strategy to ensure generalization and robustness of the method.


## Question1: Model selection.

Answer: The primary focus of this work is to propose a novel semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework along with an effective learning strategy. We believe that our method is not only applicable to SAM, but also has the potential to be transferred to other foundational vision models. Therefore, we choose to start from the original SAM to better reflect the universality of the model and to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Under this innovative framework design, the aforementioned foundational model is of course replaceable. On the one hand, MedSAM is a specialized medical segmentation model obtained by fine-tuning the original SAM on a large amount of medical image data. In theory, using it as the initial teacher model could potentially further enhance the performance of our method. On the other hand, to our knowledge, MedSAM relies on bounding boxes as prompt inputs, while our method addresses the issue of "inaccurate prompts degrading SAM performance" by feeding no prompts and updating the default embedding during training. This is another reason why we chose to build upon the original SAM rather than directly adopting MedSAM.


## Question2: Details on default embeddings.

Answer: When no prompts are provided, the prompt encoder outputs a dense prompt embedding with the shape (batch_size, embed_dim, H, W), where embed_dim matches the channel dimension of intermediate features in the mask decoder and the image embeddings from the Image Encoder, and H, W denote the spatial dimensions. This prompt dense embedding is obtained by broadcasting a learnable default embedding, which is then added to the image embeddings and fed into the mask decoder to assist in generating the final mask predictions. Thanks for your reminder and suggestion. We will include a detailed description of the default embedding in the future version of our paper.


## Question3: KL divergence on feature maps.

Answer: In Equation (3), we apply a softmax operation along the channel dimension of the feature maps to convert the feature representation at each spatial location into a probability distribution. Specifically, let $\mathbf{s}$ and $\mathbf{t}$ denote the intermediate feature maps from the student and teacher models, respectively. We first compute their corresponding probability distributions as follows:

$$
p_s = \mathrm{Softmax}(\mathbf{s}), \quad
p_t = \mathrm{Softmax}(\mathbf{t})
$$

Then, the KL divergence between the student and teacher distributions is computed at each spatial location and averaged across the entire feature map and batch:

$$ L_{\mathrm{embedding}} = D_{KL}({p_s} \mid\mid p_t) = \sum p_s \log\left(\frac{p_s}{p_t}\right)   $$

No additional projection layers are introduced in this process, in order to avoid introducing extra hyperparameters.


## Question4: Design of dynamic loss weighting.

Answer: Our designed dynamic loss weighting strategy automatically adjusts the distillation weight based on the comparison of the supervised loss performance between the student and teacher models on labeled data. Specifically, the teacher model, which has a larger capacity, is fine-tuned and then frozen at the start of training to serve as a relatively stable reference. The student model, having a smaller capacity, continuously updates its parameters during training using both labeled and unlabeled data, progressively improving its performance. At the early stage of training, since the student model's performance is weaker, its loss is typically higher than that of the teacher model, and at this time, the distillation weight $\lambda_{kd}$ remains unchanged. As training progresses, when the student's performance approaches or surpasses that of the teacher, that is, when the student's loss is lower than the teacher's loss, the distillation weight $\lambda_{kd}$ is multiplied by a scaling factor and gradually reduced.


## Question5: Comparative experimental results on the LA dataset.

Answer: Out of eight evaluation metrics under two ratio settings, we achieve the best performance on five metrics. Therefore, the statement "As shown in Table 1, our approach outperforms these competitors" in the paper is intended to reflect the overall and comprehensive performance. In fact, our main contribution lies in the innovation of the framework design and learning strategy, whereas BCP focuses more on detailed data processing techniques.


## Question6: Fine-tuning the teacher model with both labeled and unlabeled data.

Answer: Thanks for your reminder and suggestion. We carefully consider fine-tuning the teacher SAM using both labeled and unlabeled data and design the following new training pipeline. Specifically, we first perform preliminary fine-tuning on the teacher model using the labeled data. Then, the fine-tuned teacher is used to generate high-confidence pseudo-labels for the unlabeled data. Finally, we iteratively optimize the teacher model using a mixture of labeled and unlabeled data, supervised respectively by ground-truth and the previously generated pseudo-labels. However, the experimental results (see Table 2) indicate that this approach yields limited performance gains for the teacher SAM. We attribute this to the instability in the quality of pseudo-labels, which may introduce noisy information and mislead the optimization process. In addition, this method incurs substantial computational overhead and involves a more complex training pipeline, making it less efficient overall.

summary.value: The paper presents a semi-supervised segmentation method for the Segment Anything Model (SAM) which distills a standard SAM segmentation backbone to a more efficient one, using both labeled and unlabeled images. As in standard Teacher-to-Student distillation approaches for semi-supervised learning (SSL), the predictions of the Teacher for unlabeled images are used as pseudo-supervision to train the student, in addition to a standard supervised segmentation loss on labeled images. Two main modifications are made to this approach. First, a distillation loss is applied to both the output of the image encoder and the segmentation decoder. Second, the distillation transfers knowledge from the Teacher to a more efficient Student backbone. The proposed method also introduces a fine-tuning step to learn task-specific features and a dynamic adjustment of the distillation loss during SSL training. The method is evaluated on Left Atrium (LA), Brats-2019, PROMISE12 and Synapse datasets, achieving a better performance than recent SSL approaches for medical image segmentation.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

* Existing works typically use Teacher-to-Student knowledge distillation for learning a more efficient model or to obtain pseudo-labels for unlabeled examples. As mentioned in the paper, a contribution of the proposed method is to do both these steps in a single framework.

* The proposed method achieved outstanding performance on a varied set of segmentation datasets.

* The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

Weaknesses:

* Despite the contributions mentioned above, the methodological novelty of the proposed approach remains somewhat limited, as it combines two well-known distillation strategies in a single framework. 

* Although the method outperforms strong SSL baselines, the comparison is a bit tricky since most (if not all) of these baselines are based on a CNN backbone, while the method employs a transformer (ViT-B) backbone. 

* Some recently published papers report a better performance than those in the paper, for example: "DyCON: Dynamic Uncertainty-aware Consistency and Contrastive Learning for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation". I understand that the paper was put on Arxiv one month before the NeurIPS deadline, so I do not blame authors for this omission.

* The ablation study shows that the method's performance is affected by the choice of hyperparameters, such as lamba_out and lambda_emb. However, unless I missed that part, it is unclear how these hyperparameters were selected (if a validation set was employed and if they were tuned specifically for each dataset).

questions.value:
* The proposed method starts with a pre-trained SAM model which is fine-tuned to specific medical image segmentation tasks. Why not start with a model pre-trained on medical images, such as MedSAM ?

* Can authors provide more information on the default embeddings for their mask decoder (size, which decoder inputs, etc.) ?  

* In eq (3), how do you compute the KL divergence between feature maps? Do you add a learnable projector + softmax to map features into probability distributions?

* For dynamic loss weighting, two factors can impact the performance difference between the Teacher and Student: 1) the model capacity (the Teacher has a greater capacity), and 2) access to training gradient from unlabeled images (only the Student). How can you separate these two factors when choosing lambda_kd?

* In Section 4.1: " As shown in Table 1, our approach outperforms these competitors". Technically, BCP is better in terms of surface-to-surface error (HD and ASD).

* Instead of the proposed method, it would also be possible to fine-tune the SAM-based Teacher with both labeled and unlabeled data, and only after perform distillation. Has this approach been tested? If so, how does it compare?

summary.value:
Existing Challenge 1: Annotated medical imaging data is scarce and expensive to obtain.  Approach: Leverage unlabeled data for semi-supervised learning to reduce reliance on annotated data.

Existing Challenge 2: Although foundational vision models like SAM demonstrate strong generalization in general segmentation tasks, their direct application to medical images often results in suboptimal performance.  Approach: Fine-tune the original SAM using a small amount of labeled data to serve as a teacher network, and then use knowledge distillation to train a more lightweight SAM variant (student network) with the help of unlabeled data.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The Related Work and Methodology are clearly written and easy to follow. However, the claimed innovation is questionable. The authors state that the core contribution lies in leveraging unlabeled data for semi-supervised learning. Actually, unlabeled data is only used for knowledge distillation and not for effectively improving SAM's adaptation to the target domain.

Overall, the work does not constitute a true semi-supervised learning framework. The teacher network is fine-tuned using labeled data, while the student network is trained with hard labels and distills knowledge by aligning soft predictions on unlabeled data with those from the teacher. Unlabeled data serves merely as a medium for distillation, rather than directly enhancing the model’s generalization ability.

Moreover, the paper lacks critical experiments, such as evaluating the performance of the teacher network itself and quantifying the performance gap between the teacher and student networks.

questions.value:
1.	Effectiveness of the teacher network:
Knowledge distillation is essentially a model compression technique where the performance of the student network is inherently dependent on the quality of the teacher. If the teacher network performs poorly, the student network is unlikely to perform well either. Therefore, the paper should provide evidence of the teacher network’s effectiveness. 

2.	Impact of fine-tuning the teacher network:
The paper adopts a static teacher network, which is obtained by fine-tuning SAM on labeled data and then freezing it. To validate the effect of fine-tuning, the paper should compare the performance of the original SAM and the fine-tuned SAM. 

3.	Clarification on the role of unlabeled data:
The role of unlabeled data in the framework needs further clarification. In Section 3.3, the paper states: “After fine-tuning, we further optimize the model through semi-supervised learning.” What does this “optimization” refer to exactly? Is the unlabeled data only used to help align the student’s predictions with those of the teacher?

4.	Evaluation of model deployment and storage optimization:
Although the paper claims that the proposed model has less than 10% of the original SAM parameters, it does not provide a clear comparison of actual storage sizes (e.g., in MB or GB), nor does it report key deployment metrics such as inference speed or latency in clinical scenarios.

5.	Does offline distillation limit the model's adaptability?
The teacher model is frozen after fine-tuning, while the student model continues to be updated during training. This offline distillation approach may prevent the teacher from adapting to the student’s evolving learning status or distribution shift. Has the author considered using a soft update strategy (e.g., EMA) to enhance the adaptability of the model?

Both the teacher and student models are trained on the same labeled data, and the student model additionally learns from the pseudo-labels and intermediate features generated by the teacher. I still do not understand why the student model would outperform the teacher.

summary.value: This paper presents a novel fully SAM-based semi-supervised medical image segmentation (SSMIS) framework designed to address the scarcity of annotated medical imaging data. It tackles the suboptimal performance of generalist SAM models on medical images by integrating an efficient SAM variant as the backbone and updating its default prompt embedding.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths:**
1. The paper proposes a novel framework that fully leverages an efficient SAM variant as the backbone for semi-supervised medical image segmentation.
2. The sophisticated knowledge distillation strategy from an original SAM teacher to optimize the efficient student SAM backbone is interesting.
3. It updates SAM's default prompt embedding, and mitigate the negative impact of inaccurate prompts.

**Weakness:**
1. The student model's performance is inherently tied to the capabilities of the original SAM teacher. If the teacher, even after fine-tuning on medical data, struggles with certain rare pathologies or complex anatomical variations, these limitations will be propagated, potentially capping the student's accuracy in critical cases.
2. While "various medical datasets" are mentioned, the specific range of medical imaging modalities (e.g., MRI, CT, X-ray, ultrasound, different anatomical regions, varying image qualities) and their pathological diversity are not explicitly detailed in the abstract. SAM's generalization can still be challenging across wildly different medical image characteristics.

questions.value:
1. Could the authors provide a more granular breakdown of the "various medical datasets" used, specifying modalities, anatomical regions, and the range of pathological conditions to better assess the true generalizability?
2. How sensitive is the model's performance to the choice of distillation strategy parameters and the dynamic loss weighting schedule? Is there an automated way to tune these, or does it require significant manual effort per dataset?

limitations.value:
1. **teacher-student model dependency:** The fundamental effectiveness of the proposed semi-supervised framework relies on the "teacher" (original SAM) providing accurate and rich knowledge. If the teacher struggles with the inherent complexities, ambiguities, or out-of-distribution characteristics of certain medical images, the student's performance will be capped, potentially leading to critical errors in clinical diagnoses or interventions.
2. **generalizability to highly fiverse medical modalities/anatomies:** Medical imaging is incredibly diverse. A model performing well on one type of medical data (e.g., cardiac MRI) may not directly generalize to another (e.g., lung CT scans with diffuse pathologies) due to different image characteristics and anatomical contexts. This limits the "plug-and-play" nature of the solution for broad clinical applicability and necessitates careful validation for each new application.
3. **complexity of hierarchical knowledge transfer and dynamic weighting:** The intricate distillation and weighting mechanisms, while contributing to performance, increase the complexity of model development and deployment. Achieving optimal results likely requires expert-level hyperparameter tuning, which could be a barrier for wider adoption in clinical research or practice where ease of use is paramount.

title.value: Segment Anything Model Meets Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation: A Novel Perspective

abstract.value: The scarcity of annotated medical imaging data has driven significant progress in semi-supervised learning to alleviate reliance on expensive expert labeling. While foundational vision models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) exhibit robust generalization in generic segmentation tasks, their direct application to medical images often results in suboptimal performance. To address this challenge, in this work, we propose a novel fully SAM-based semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework and develop the corresponding knowledge distillation-based learning strategy. Specifically, we first employ an efficient SAM variant as the backbone network of the semi‑supervised framework and update the default prompt embedding of SAM to unleash its full potential. Then, we utilize an original SAM, which is rich in prior knowledge, as the teacher to optimize our efficient student SAM backbone through hierarchical knowledge distillation and a dynamic loss weighting strategy. Extensive experiments on various medical datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation approaches. Especially, our model requires less than 10% of the parameter size of the original SAM, enabling substantially lower deployment and storage overhead in real-world clinical settings.
